newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal farmers seek compensation for crop losses.
newsitem.headline: Portugal farmers seek compensation for crop losses.

text.p: Recent rain will not save Portugal's winter cereal crops, ravaged by drought, and the main farmers' group has urged the Socialist government to compensate farmers, its president said on Wednesday.
"Rain levels have been more than 50 percent below normal this year," Jose Andrade, president of the Confederation of Portuguese Farmers (CAP), told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"Recent rain has been sporadic and will have no effect on the cereal harvest this summer. The overall situation is extremely worrying, especially for cattle rearing," he said.

The CAP, which represents most of Portugal's 460,000 farmers, had submitted a document to the government on Monday asking for cuts in tax and social security payments and direct income support for farmers nationwide hit by the drought.

Andrade said the CAP had asked the government to release money from the so-called 'calamities fund' for farmers who had paid voluntary insurance premiums into the fund. The CAP had yet to receive a response from the government.
Andrade estimated that just 7,000 farmers had paid into the calamities fund and would be eligible to receive compensation from the fund.
Agriculture Ministry spokesman Augusto Vilela said he could not rule out possible payments from the calamities fund.
"The government is coming under immense political pressure to pay out from the calamities fund," he said.
Estimates of the value of the fund, set up a year ago, were not immediately available.
A senior government official said last month one of the worst winter droughts in the last 150 years had destroyed an estimated 50 to 70 percent of Portugal's winter cereal crops.
Deputy Secretary of State for Agriculture Carlos Cunha said rain in Portugal's southern cereal-producing Alentejo region might save pasture but not winter crops, predominantly wheat.
In 1996 Portugal, Europe's smallest cereals producer, harvested around 415,000 tonnes of wheat, up from 360,000 tonnes the previous year.

Andrade said he could not estimate accurately how much of Portugal's winter cereals crop had been lost. But production had been almost wiped out in some parts of the Alentejo as well as in the central Beira Interior and northern Tras Os Montes regions.
